summary: This note describes Bison antiquus, an extinct North American bison species that lived until about 10,000 years ago and was a direct ancestor of the living American bison. It traces the species' evolutionary lineage from steppe wisent migrating over the Bering Land Bridge through B. latifrons. It also gives the species' abundance, notable La Brea tar pit fossils, and size measurements relative to modern bison.
one_line: Bison antiquus was an extinct, larger North American bison species and direct ancestor of the living American bison.
key_facts: Steppe wisent (B. priscus) migrated from Siberia into Alaska across the Bering Land Bridge between 240,000 and 220,000 years ago during the later Pleistocene epoch.
Bison priscus evolved into long-horned bison, B. latifrons, in western North America.
B. latifrons evolved into B. antiquus, and the larger B. latifrons appears to have died out by about 20,000 ya.
B. antiquus became increasingly abundant in parts of midcontinent North America from 18,000 ya until about 10,000 ya.
After about 10,000 ya, B. antiquus appears to have given rise to the living species, B. bison.
B. antiquus is the most commonly recovered large mammalian herbivore from the La Brea tar pits.
B. antiquus was 15-25% larger overall than modern bison.
B. antiquus reached up to 2.27 m (7.5 ft) tall.
B. antiquus reached up to 4.6 m (15 ft) long.
B. antiquus reached a weight of up to 1,588 kg (3500 lb).
From tip to tip, the horns of B. antiquus measured about 3 ft (nearly 1 m).
B. antiquus had taller stature, larger bones and larger horns than modern bison.
Bison antiquus is described as an extinct species of bison that lived in North America until around 10,000 years ago.
B. antiquus was one of the most common large herbivores on the North American continent during the late Pleistocene.
